stem: A new wireless deployment must resist the offline guessing that hurts a captured WPA2-Personal handshake, and the company can replace the clients. RADIUS is not ready. Which protection is designed for that gap?
choices: WPA3-Personal with SAE
WEP with a longer key
An open network with a hidden name
Telnet for the passphrase exchange
explanation: WPA3-Personal uses SAE so a captured handshake is not a free offline guess against the passphrase. Hiding the SSID does not change the handshake. WEP is weaker. Telnet is clear-text remote login and is not a Wi-Fi key exchange. Enterprise with RADIUS is stronger still when they are ready for per-user accounts.
choiceNotes: SAE is the WPA3-Personal method aimed at that offline-guessing problem.
WEP is obsolete and broken. A longer WEP key is not the upgrade.
A hidden name is not encryption and not a modern handshake.
Telnet exposes sessions. It does not replace a Wi-Fi handshake.

stem: A web application sets a session cookie. Script on the page must not be able to read it, and the cookie must not be sent over clear-text HTTP. Which two cookie flags address those two requirements? (Choose two.)
choices: HttpOnly
Secure
A flag that stores the password in the cookie in clear text
A flag that disables TLS
explanation: HttpOnly tells the browser not to expose the cookie to script, which limits the damage of cross-site scripting. Secure tells the browser to send the cookie only over HTTPS. Putting the password in the cookie undoes the point of a session identifier. Disabling TLS removes the protection the Secure flag depends on.
choiceNotes: HttpOnly keeps document-level script from reading the session cookie.
The Secure flag withholds the cookie from non-HTTPS requests.
A clear-text password in a cookie is a credential leak, not a flag you want.
Disabling TLS makes the Secure flag meaningless and exposes the session.

stem: A build server refuses to deploy a binary that is not signed by the release key. A developer asks for the check to be turned off 'just for this hotfix.' What is the control, and why does the exception matter?
choices: Code signing. An unsigned hotfix is exactly what the check exists to stop
Code signing proves the binary has no bugs
Turning the check off is fine if the developer is in a hurry
Signatures encrypt the binary for confidentiality
explanation: A signature shows the binary came from a holder of the release key and was not swapped later. It does not prove the code is free of bugs. The hotfix path should sign the binary, not skip the check. A skipped check is how a tampered hotfix lands. Signing is integrity and origin, not confidentiality.
choiceNotes: Keep the check and sign the hotfix. The hurry is not a reason to accept an unsigned binary.
A signature does not review logic. It answers 'who produced this and has it changed,' not 'is it correct.'
The exception is the hole. Attackers and mistakes both use the unsigned path.
Encryption would hide the bytes. A signature leaves them readable and verifies them.

stem: A server image still has the vendor administrator password and three network services nobody uses. Hardening starts with which two actions? (Choose two.)
choices: Change the default password
Disable the unused services
Publish the new password in a public chat
Add the server to an any-any firewall rule
explanation: Default passwords are published, and unused services are extra code you must patch and that attackers can try. Change the password and turn the services off before the image is cloned. Publishing the password and opening any-any undo the hardening.
choiceNotes: The vendor password is public knowledge until you change it.
An unused service is attack surface. Disable it and remove the firewall rule that existed for it.
A public chat is a broadcast of the secret.
Any-any allows the traffic the hardening was meant to refuse.

stem: Static review of source finds a query built from user input. A separate test runs the compiled application and sends unexpected input. Which names match those two activities?
choices: Static analysis, then dynamic testing
Dynamic testing, then a code review that never runs
Both are penetration tests of the production network
Both are hardware inventories
explanation: Static analysis inspects the code without running it. Dynamic testing runs it. They catch different things: static review can see the dangerous concatenation, and dynamic testing can see what the running app actually does. Neither one is automatically a production penetration test, and neither inventories hardware.
choiceNotes: Reading the source is static. Running the app is dynamic. Do both.
The running test is the dynamic one. The source review is static, whether or not you also execute it.
A production penetration test is an authorized exercise against live or production-like systems under rules of engagement. A code review is earlier.
Hardware inventory counts devices. It does not read queries.

stem: A laptop is assigned to one employee, tracked in the inventory, and the employee is recorded as the user. Security still cannot say who owns the data on it or who must approve a wipe. What asset field is missing?
choices: An owner, distinct from the person who happens to be using the device
A second identical serial number
Permission for anyone to wipe it without a record
Removal of the device from the inventory so it is 'simpler'
explanation: The owner is accountable for the asset and the data. The user is the person holding it today. Those are different roles. A wipe, a transfer, and a classification decision need an owner. Duplicate serials and silent wipes destroy accountability. Dropping it from inventory hides the asset.
choiceNotes: Name an owner. The current user is not automatically the person who may approve destruction of the data.
Two serial numbers make the inventory lie. They do not create ownership.
An unrecorded wipe is how data disappears without a decision.
An asset you remove from inventory is an asset you cannot protect or recover.

stem: A spinning disk and an SSD are leaving the building. Degaussing is available. A certificate of destruction is required by the lease return. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Degaussing can destroy the magnetic disk. It is not a reliable wipe for the SSD. Get a certificate for the method you actually use
Degaussing is the preferred wipe for every SSD
A quick format satisfies a certificate of destruction
Throwing both drives in the trash produces the certificate
explanation: Degaussing scrambles magnetic media. SSDs do not store data that way, so the reliable options are a vendor cryptographic erase or physical destruction. A certificate describes what was done by whom. A quick format does not earn one. A trash can is not a process.
choiceNotes: Degauss the magnetic drive if that is your method, and destroy or cryptographically erase the SSD. Certificate the real method.
A degausser is the wrong tool to trust for flash. Do not batch the SSD in and assume it is clean.
A quick format leaves recoverable data. It is not destruction.
Trash produces no chain of custody and no certificate.

stem: An SSD is encrypted with a key stored in a secure module. Sanitization destroys that key and leaves the encrypted bytes in place. Why can this be an acceptable purge when a full overwrite would take hours?
choices: Without the key the ciphertext is not recoverable. This is cryptographic erase
Destroying the key decrypts the drive for the next owner
Cryptographic erase works even if the drive was never encrypted
The method prints the key on the certificate so the next owner can read the disk
explanation: Cryptographic erase relies on the encryption having been real and the key being the only copy. Destroy the key and the leftover ciphertext is noise. It does nothing for a drive that was never encrypted. The certificate should say the key was destroyed, not include the key. Overwriting is still appropriate when you cannot trust the encryption.
choiceNotes: The data was already ciphertext. Losing the only key is the purge. Confirm there is no escrow copy you forgot.
Destroying the key does not decrypt anything. It does the opposite.
If the bytes were never encrypted, deleting a key that does not exist leaves plaintext in place.
Putting the key on the certificate gives the next reader the secret. The certificate attests to destruction.

stem: A department keeps every file forever because 'storage is cheap,' including data the policy says to delete after seven years. What asset and data practice is failing?
choices: Retention. Keeping data past the policy increases exposure and can violate the policy
Retention requires keeping regulated records for one day
A shorter retention than the policy demands is always safer, including for records you must keep
Inventory is the same thing as retention
explanation: Retention is how long you keep something and when you destroy it. Keeping everything forever means a breach includes data you had a duty to delete, and it can break the policy or the law. Deleting too soon is the opposite failure when a record must be kept. Inventory tells you what you have. Retention tells you how long it may stay.
choiceNotes: Delete on the schedule. Extra years are extra breach impact and sometimes a compliance miss.
One day is not a universal retention period. The policy and the regulation set the time.
Some records must be kept. Destroying them early is its own violation.
Inventory is the list. Retention is the clock. You need both.

stem: A scanner reports a critical finding. An engineer proves the vulnerable feature is not installed, and the banner the scanner matched was a cosmetic string. What is the finding?
choices: A false positive
A false negative
A zero-day
A confirmed exploitable hole
explanation: A false positive is a report of a problem you do not have. You still document why you closed it. A false negative is a real problem the scanner missed, which is worse. A zero-day is an unfixed unknown flaw. A cosmetic banner is not, by itself, a hole. Do not ignore the scanner. Tune it and keep the evidence.
choiceNotes: The scanner was wrong. Close it as a false positive and, if the banner is useless, stop publishing the confusing string.
A false negative would be a real flaw the scanner did not mention. This is the opposite.
A zero-day is not a scanner mismatch on a feature you do not run.
The engineer showed the feature is absent. That is not a confirmed hole.

stem: CVE-2024-12345 has a CVSS score of 9.8. The affected service is not exposed and the asset holds no sensitive data. A different finding scores 6.5 on a payroll server that is reachable by every user. Why is 'patch the 9.8 first' incomplete?
choices: CVSS is severity of the vulnerability, not your risk. Exposure and asset value can make the 6.5 more urgent here
CVSS already includes your payroll process, so the 9.8 must go first
Scores under 7.0 can be ignored forever
CVE numbers sort the work. Higher numbers are older and always wait
explanation: CVSS describes the vulnerability in a generic environment: how bad is the bug if it is attacked. It does not know that your payroll server is the one users can reach. Risk uses that context. You might still patch the 9.8 quickly if exposure changes. You do not sort only by the base score, and you do not ignore 6.5 on payroll. CVE identifiers are labels, not priority.
choiceNotes: Use the score as input. Then ask what the asset is and who can reach it. Payroll wins this comparison.
Base CVSS does not know your org chart or your network. That is why a risk decision is still required.
A 6.5 on payroll is not ignorable. The threshold idea throws away context.
CVE numbers identify issues. They are not a chronological to-do list.

stem: After a patch, the ticket is closed with no further scan. The next audit finds the old version still running on half the hosts. What step was skipped?
choices: Validation, a rescan or other proof that the fix is actually in place
Writing a longer CVE identifier
Disabling the scanner so it cannot disagree
Announcing the patch before it was tested, as a substitute for the rescan
explanation: Remediation is not done when the package is 'approved.' Validation checks that the hosts actually took it. A rescan, a version query, or a configuration check is that proof. A longer identifier does not patch anything. Disabling the scanner hides the miss. An announcement is not evidence.
choiceNotes: Rescan or query the versions. Half the fleet missing the patch is why this step exists.
The CVE string is a name. Lengthening it does not deploy software.
Turning the scanner off preserves the false sense that the ticket is done.
Telling people you patched is not a measurement of the hosts.

stem: A researcher tells the company about a flaw privately and waits for a fix before publishing. A different program pays outsiders to test a defined scope and report what they find. What are those two practices?
choices: Responsible disclosure, and a bug bounty
A watering hole, and tailgating
A honeyfile, and a CRL
Shadow IT, and a cold site
explanation: Responsible disclosure is the private report and the wait. A bug bounty is a paid, scoped program. Both are ways findings arrive without a surprise dump. They are not attacks, decoys, or recovery sites. A bounty still needs rules of engagement, a scope, and a safe harbor so testers are not treated as intruders.
choiceNotes: Private notice plus time to fix is responsible disclosure. The paid scoped program is the bounty.
A watering hole and tailgating are attack techniques, not reporting practices.
A honeyfile is a decoy. A CRL is a revocation list.
Shadow IT and a cold site are an unsanctioned app and a recovery room.

stem: A penetration test is authorized. The testers are given no credentials and no network map. A second test gives them a standard user account and a diagram. Which environments are those, in the current Security+ wording?
choices: Unknown environment, then partially known environment
Known environment, then a test with no rules
Both unknown, because testers are outsiders
A tabletop, then a cryptographic erase
explanation: Unknown means the tester starts with little or no internal knowledge, the old 'black box.' Partially known means some access or some documentation, the old 'gray box.' Known means the tester has deep internal detail. Rules of engagement still apply to all of them. A tabletop does not send packets. Cryptographic erase deletes keys.
choiceNotes: No credentials and no map is unknown. An account plus a diagram is partially known.
Known would hand over substantial internal detail, such as source or admin access. 'No rules' is not a test type.
Being an outside firm does not define the environment. The information you give them does.
A tabletop is a meeting. Cryptographic erase is sanitization. Neither is this pair of tests.

stem: Firewall, VPN, and server authentication logs are shipped to one system that can search them together and alert when a VPN login is followed by a denied firewall hit. What is that system?
choices: A SIEM
A badge printer
A degausser
A cold site
explanation: A SIEM aggregates and correlates logs. The sequence 'VPN then a deny' is a correlation rule, not something you see in one device's local buffer. A badge printer, a degausser, and a cold site do not search logs. Shipping the logs off the server also helps when a host's local log is later cleared.
choiceNotes: Correlation across device types is the SIEM's job. Write the rule and keep the logs off-box.
A badge printer makes cards. It does not correlate a VPN and a firewall.
A degausser destroys magnetic media. It does not alert.
A cold site is an empty recovery location.

stem: Analysts ignore a noisy alert that fires hundreds of times a day for a known scanner. A real attack later uses the same alert and nobody pages. What failure is that?
choices: Alert fatigue from an untuned rule
A SIEM that is too quiet
Perfect tuning, because the scanner is allowed to hide later attacks
A physical bollard
explanation: Alert fatigue is what happens when noisy rules train people to click past them. Tune the scanner into a lower severity or an exception that does not match the attack pattern, and test that the real pattern still pages. Silence is not success. A bollard does not triage alerts.
choiceNotes: Tune the rule so the known scanner is identifiable and the unexpected source still alarms. Fatigue is the outage in the process.
The problem is too much noise, not too little. Quiet would be a different failure.
An exception that hides every future use of the technique is not tuning. It is blindness.
A bollard does not sit in the alert queue.

stem: A report needs to show which hosts talked to a suspicious address and how many bytes moved. It does not need the payload. Full packet capture of the core would be enormous. Which source fits?
choices: Flow records such as NetFlow or IPFIX
A screenshot of a desktop
A CRL
A password hash database
explanation: Flow records summarize conversations: addresses, ports, bytes, and timing. They answer 'who talked and how much' without storing every packet. Packet capture is what you add when you need the payload, under a narrower scope. A screenshot, a revocation list, and a hash database do not describe traffic.
choiceNotes: Flow data is the right weight for who-talked-to-whom. Start there.
A screenshot of a desktop is not a record of who talked to whom on the network.
A CRL lists revoked certificates. It does not count bytes.
Password hashes are credentials. They are not flow records, and they do not belong in this report.

stem: An investigation needs the TLS handshake and the HTTP headers from one web server for a ten-minute window. Flow records show the conversations but not the headers. What additional source is required, and what should limit it?
choices: A packet capture on that server or a tap, limited in time and scope, with access controlled
Another year of NetFlow and no packets
A public posting of the capture so everyone can help
Disabling TLS so headers are easier, then leaving it off
explanation: Headers and handshakes are in packets, not in flow summaries. Capture the smallest useful window and protect the file, because it may contain secrets. Publishing it is a breach. Turning TLS off to make the investigation easier creates a standing exposure. Flow remains useful to decide where to capture.
choiceNotes: Capture packets for that host and that window. Then lock the file down.
NetFlow will never grow headers. More of it does not change the format.
A public capture distributes whatever the users sent. That is not an investigation method.
Disabling TLS is a production change that exposes everyone, not a way to read one incident.

stem: Endpoint software moves a suspected file out of the user's folder and stops it from executing while an analyst reviews it. What is that state?
choices: Quarantine
Publication
A hot site
Data in transit by definition
explanation: Quarantine isolates a suspect object without immediately deleting it, so you can recover from a false positive and so the object cannot run. Publishing it would spread it. A hot site is a recovery facility. The file is not 'in transit' just because it was moved on the same disk.
choiceNotes: Quarantine is the hold. The file cannot run, and you can still decide.
Publication is the opposite of isolation.
A hot site is a staffed recovery location.
Transit means the data is crossing a network. A local quarantine folder is not that.

stem: Mail from the company is rejected after a new cloud mail host is added. The DNS record that lists who may send still names only the old host. Which record is that?
choices: SPF
An A record for the website
A PTR record for a workstation
A CNAME for the intranet
explanation: SPF is a TXT record of the servers allowed to send for the domain. Receivers treat mail from an unlisted host as spoofing. DKIM signs messages and DMARC sets the policy, but the stem describes the sender list, which is SPF. The website's A record can be perfect and mail will still fail.
choiceNotes: Update SPF to include the new host. That is the authorization list receivers are checking.
The A record makes the website resolve. It does not authorize outbound mail.
A workstation PTR is reverse DNS for that host. It is not the domain's sender policy.
A CNAME aliases a name. It does not list mail senders.

stem: A company wants mail that fails SPF or DKIM alignment to be rejected, and wants reports about those failures. Which policy layer states that?
choices: DMARC
WEP
A screensaver
A bollard
explanation: DMARC tells receivers what to do when SPF or DKIM fail to align with the visible from-address, and it can request reports. SPF and DKIM are the checks DMARC builds on. You publish DMARC only after those checks are correct, or you will reject your own mail. WEP, a screensaver, and a bollard are not mail policy.
choiceNotes: DMARC is the policy and the reporting. Get SPF and DKIM right first, then set the disposition.
WEP is obsolete Wi-Fi. It does not reject mail.
A screensaver locks a console. It does not tell receivers to reject mail.
A bollard stops vehicles in a driveway. It does not set mail policy.

stem: Laptops that fail a health check, missing a required update, are placed on a network where they can reach only the update servers. Healthy laptops reach the office. What capability is that?
choices: Network access control
A public DNS resolver with no policy
Degaussing
A cold site
explanation: NAC checks posture and then admits, redirects, or denies. The remediation network is the redirect. It is not a punishment VLAN you forget about. It exists so the laptop can become healthy. A public resolver, a degausser, and a cold site do not check patch level at connection time.
choiceNotes: NAC is the admission decision. The limited network is how a failing laptop gets the update it lacks.
A public resolver answers names for anyone. It does not inspect laptop health.
Degaussing destroys magnetic media. It does not steer a laptop to a patch server.
A cold site is a recovery room, not an admission control.

stem: Endpoint detection and response software records process trees and can isolate a laptop. A traditional antivirus product on the same fleet mainly matches file signatures. What does EDR add that signature antivirus does not?
choices: Behavioral telemetry and a way to investigate and contain a host, including activity that has no known file signature
A guarantee that signatures are unnecessary and can be deleted
Replacement of identity and access management
Physical badges
explanation: EDR watches what processes do and keeps that history, so an analyst can see a chain that never matched a file hash. Isolation is a response action. Signatures still catch known malware quickly. You do not throw them away. EDR does not issue directory accounts or print badges.
choiceNotes: Behavior and response are the addition. A fileless or renamed technique can show up in the process tree without a signature hit.
Signatures remain useful. EDR does not make them garbage.
IAM is accounts and access. An endpoint agent does not replace joiner-mover-leaver.
Badges are physical. EDR does not issue them.

stem: A proxy blocks a category of sites and also inspects files that users upload for strings that look like customer account numbers. Which two capabilities are those?
choices: Web filtering, and data loss prevention
A jump server, and a degausser
RAID 0, and a cold site
A salt, and a CRL
explanation: Web filtering decides which sites or categories are allowed. DLP looks at the content for sensitive data leaving or being posted. A proxy can host both, and they are still two controls. A jump server, a degausser, RAID, a salt, and a CRL do not classify URLs or account numbers.
choiceNotes: Category blocking is web filtering. The account-number check is DLP.
A jump server is an admin path. A degausser wipes magnetic disks.
RAID 0 stripes disks with no redundancy. A cold site is an empty recovery room.
A salt is for password hashes. A CRL lists revoked certificates.

stem: File integrity monitoring alerts because a system binary changed hash and no change ticket exists. What is the alert telling you?
choices: A protected file changed outside the approved process. Investigate before you accept the new hash
The hash change is automatically benign
Integrity monitoring encrypts the file
You should update the baseline first and investigate never
explanation: Integrity monitoring detects unexpected change. A binary that changes with no ticket might be a patch someone forgot to record, or it might be a replacement. You compare the change to the ticket and the vendor package before you bless the new hash. Updating the baseline first teaches the tool that the unknown change is normal.
choiceNotes: Investigate, then update the baseline only if the change was legitimate.
An unexplained binary change is not benign until you show that it is.
A hash comparison does not encrypt. It detects modification.
Accepting the hash first destroys the evidence that anything was unexpected.

stem: A terminated employee's account still works the next day, and their laptop is still enrolled. Which identity process failed?
choices: Deprovisioning
Hiring, which should be slower
Salting
A tabletop
explanation: Deprovisioning removes access when the relationship ends: account, tokens, VPN, laptop, badges. Leaving it for a day is a window. Hiring is the opposite process. Salting is a hashing technique. A tabletop is an exercise. The checklist should be automatic enough that a Friday termination does not wait for Monday.
choiceNotes: Disable the account and pull the devices and tokens. Deprovisioning is that process.
Hiring grants access. The failure is on the way out.
Salting does not enable or disable accounts.
A tabletop discusses a scenario. It does not disable this user.

stem: Users sign in once to an identity provider and reach several web applications because those applications trust a signed assertion. Which technology is the usual enterprise web assertion?
choices: SAML
A DHCP lease
WEP
A bollard
explanation: SAML carries a signed authentication assertion from an identity provider to an application. That is a common enterprise single sign-on pattern. OAuth is a different conversation, about delegated authorization. DHCP, WEP, and bollards do not log a user into a web app.
choiceNotes: SAML is the assertion. The applications trust the identity provider instead of each collecting a password.
A DHCP lease is an address. It is not a login.
WEP is obsolete Wi-Fi encryption. It does not sign a user into a web application.
A bollard is a vehicle barrier. It does not carry a login assertion.

stem: A mobile app asks a user to approve access to their cloud files, and the app then calls the cloud API with a token. The app never learned the user's password. The token is not, by itself, proof of who the user is to a third site. Which protocol family is the delegated access?
choices: OAuth 2.0 for authorization. OpenID Connect would be what adds an identity layer
OAuth, which by itself is always the authentication of the user to every website
A CRL
RAID 1
explanation: OAuth 2.0 delegates access: the user approves a scope and the app gets a token. It is an authorization framework. OpenID Connect sits on OAuth and provides an identity token so an application can know who signed in. Treating raw OAuth as authentication is a common design bug. A CRL and RAID are unrelated.
choiceNotes: The file access without the password is OAuth's delegated authorization. Identity for login is OpenID Connect on top of that.
OAuth alone does not identify the user to an arbitrary site. Using it that way is the mix-up.
A CRL lists revoked certificates. It does not grant a cloud-file scope.
RAID 1 mirrors disks. It does not delegate API access or identify a user.

stem: Administrators use their personal accounts for email and a separate privileged account that has no mailbox and is used only for admin tools. Just-in-time elevation grants the privileged rights for one hour. What practices are those?
choices: Separate privileged accounts and just-in-time access
One shared administrator password for the whole team
Privilege that lasts forever once granted
Mailboxes on the privileged accounts so phishing has a place to land
explanation: Privileged access management separates the everyday identity from the dangerous one and shortens how long the dangerous rights exist. A shared password destroys accountability. Standing admin rights wait to be stolen. A mailbox on the admin account is a phishing path into the keys.
choiceNotes: Two accounts plus a short elevation is the pattern. The hour ends and the rights go away.
A shared password means you cannot say who used it, and everyone knows it.
Forever is the opposite of just-in-time.
The privileged account should not read mail. Phishing the mailbox would be phishing the admin.

stem: A service account for a backup job is also used by three people as an interactive login, and the password has not changed in five years. What is wrong?
choices: A service account should not be a shared human login, and a static password that old is a standing key
Service accounts should be domain admin and posted on the wiki
Interactive use is required so the backup can run
Five years is the recommended maximum only for user accounts, and service accounts should never rotate
explanation: Service accounts exist for a workload. People sharing them hides who did what and spreads the password. Prefer a managed identity or a frequently rotated secret, least privilege, and no interactive logon. Domain admin and a wiki post are the failure mode. Rotation applies to these secrets too.
choiceNotes: Stop the interactive use, reduce the rights, and rotate the secret. The account is for the job, not for three desktops.
Domain admin plus a wiki is how the password becomes everyone's.
The backup service can run as a service. Humans do not need to log on as it.
Long-lived service passwords are a common breach. They are not exempt from rotation.

stem: Every quarter, managers receive a list of who can read the payroll share and must confirm or remove each person. What is that review called, and what does it catch?
choices: Access recertification. It catches rights that accumulated and were never removed
A penetration test
A CRL download
A first-time hire provisioning, which removes access
explanation: Recertification, or an access review, forces an owner to look at current rights. People change jobs and keep old groups. The review is how those lingerers are removed. A penetration test is an authorized attack. A CRL is about certificates. Provisioning is how access is granted at the start, not the quarterly cleanup.
choiceNotes: The quarterly confirm-or-remove is recertification. Job changes are what it is there to catch.
A penetration test does not ask managers to attest to a share's membership.
A CRL is a list of revoked certificates, not payroll group members.
Provisioning gives access to a new hire. This review takes access away.

stem: A playbook disables an account, isolates the laptop, and opens a ticket when a high-severity detection fires. A person does not have to click through those three steps at 3 a.m. What is the benefit and the tool class?
choices: Orchestration, often SOAR, so a standard response happens quickly and the same way each time
Manual heroics, which are more consistent than a playbook
Disabling the detection so the playbook never runs
A bollard that isolates laptops
explanation: Orchestration connects systems so one detection can drive many actions. The benefit is speed and consistency. A person should still be able to review high-impact actions if the playbook can lock out a VIP by mistake. Turning off the detection avoids the response by going blind. A bollard does not isolate a laptop on the network.
choiceNotes: The playbook is orchestration. It does the same safe steps every time, including at 3 a.m.
Heroics vary by who is awake. That is less consistent, not more.
Disabling the detection removes the signal the playbook needs.
A bollard is a physical barrier. Network isolation is an API call.

stem: All account creation flows through one automation platform. The platform is down, and nobody has a documented manual path. New hires cannot work, and emergency access cannot be granted. What did the design forget?
choices: The automation is a single point of failure and needs a break-glass procedure
Automation should be impossible to bypass even when it is down
Manual paths should use a shared administrator password posted in chat
Identity is less important during an outage
explanation: Automation concentrates process. If that process is the only path, its outage is an identity outage. Break-glass access is a monitored, short-lived, heavily logged exception for exactly this case. 'Impossible to bypass' strands the business. A shared password in chat is not a break-glass design. Identity matters more during an outage, not less.
choiceNotes: Write and test a break-glass path, and alert whenever it is used. The platform will fail eventually.
A control you cannot bypass when it is broken becomes an outage of its own.
A posted shared password is a standing backdoor, not an emergency procedure.
An outage is when inappropriate access is most tempting. Keep identity in the procedure.

stem: A pipeline deploys infrastructure only from reviewed templates and refuses a change that would open a management port to the world. What is that refusal?
choices: A guard rail
A honeypot
Alert fatigue
A cold backup
explanation: Guard rails are automated checks that keep people inside a safe set of configurations. The refused rule is the rail working. The developer can request an exception through a reviewed path. A honeypot, fatigue, and a cold backup do not block a template.
choiceNotes: The pipeline constraint is a guard rail. It encodes 'we do not publish management ports' so a tired deploy cannot.
A honeypot is a decoy system. It does not review templates.
Alert fatigue is analysts ignoring noise. This refuse is a build failure, not an ignored page.
A cold backup is a recovery copy. It does not lint firewall rules.

stem: An old script has special cases nobody understands. Every new integration copies those cases. Engineers are afraid to replace it. What long-term cost is that?
choices: Technical debt
A lower CVSS score
Data sovereignty
A shorter RPO
explanation: Technical debt is the accumulated cost of shortcuts and unexplained complexity. It shows up as fear of change and as bugs copied into the next integration. It is not a vulnerability score, a legal region, or a backup target. Paying it down is a security activity when the script is on the identity or firewall path, because fear of change means fear of patching.
choiceNotes: The fear and the copied special cases are technical debt. Schedule time to replace the script before it becomes the outage.
CVSS scores a vulnerability. It does not measure how afraid the team is of a script.
Sovereignty is about where data may live.
RPO is how much data you can lose. A shorter RPO is a tighter target, not this script.

stem: A confirmed intrusion is still running on a server that can reach the rest of the data center. The team wants to discuss lessons learned before they disconnect anything. What is out of order?
choices: Containment comes before lessons learned. Disconnect or isolate first
Lessons learned is the first technical step
Preparation happens after the intrusion is over, so it is too late to have a plan
Eradication should happen before anyone stops the spread
explanation: The response order is prepare ahead of time, then detect and analyze, contain, eradicate, recover, and only then capture lessons. Lessons learned is how you improve the plan. It is not how you stop a live spread. Preparation is the work you did before this incident. Eradication on a host that is still connected lets the attacker move while you delete files.
choiceNotes: Isolate the server. The retrospective can wait until the bleeding has stopped.
Lessons learned is the last step. Doing it first leaves the attacker connected.
Preparation is before the incident. You do not start writing the first runbook while a live host is pivoting.
Eradication before containment can tip off the attacker and can wipe evidence while the access remains.

stem: Legal says a set of mailboxes must be preserved exactly, and ordinary deletion jobs must skip them, because litigation is reasonably anticipated. What is that hold?
choices: A legal hold
A routine retention delete that ignores the instruction
A cryptographic erase of the mailboxes
A public blog post of the messages
explanation: A legal hold suspends normal destruction so evidence is not lost. Deleting anyway, cryptographically erasing, or publishing the mail are all failures of the hold. The security team does not decide the hold is inconvenient. They implement it and document that deletion was suppressed.
choiceNotes: Suppress the deletion jobs and record the hold. Preservation is the requirement.
A retention delete that skips the legal instruction destroys evidence.
Cryptographic erase is sanitization. It is the opposite of a hold.
Publishing the messages is disclosure, not preservation.

stem: A laptop is collected for an investigation. The analyst who receives it does not record who had it, when, or how it was stored overnight. A later hearing asks whether the disk image could have been altered. What process failure is that?
choices: Chain of custody
A missing screensaver
Too much documentation
A successful tabletop
explanation: Chain of custody is the record of possession and handling. Without it, the other side can argue the evidence was changed and you may not be able to answer. Write down each transfer, store the device securely, and hash images so you can show they did not change while you held them. Extra documentation is not the failure. A tabletop does not collect a laptop.
choiceNotes: Start the log at collection. Who, when, where, and the hash are what the hearing will ask for.
A screensaver is irrelevant to whether the disk image is trustworthy.
The failure is too little documentation of custody, not too much.
A tabletop is a discussion exercise. It does not establish custody of a device.

stem: Hunters search for a technique they read about in a threat report. No alert has fired. They find one host using the technique and then open an incident. How is hunting different from waiting on the SIEM?
choices: Hunting is proactive. It looks for activity that rules have not already named
Hunting waits for a page and then stops
Hunting replaces the need for any detection rules
Hunting is only legal if no one writes anything down
explanation: Threat hunting assumes some activity will not match a current rule. People form a hypothesis from intelligence and go look. When they find something, it should become a detection so the next one is not a hunt. Hunting does not replace alerts, and it should be documented like any other investigation.
choiceNotes: The search started from a hypothesis, not from a page. That is hunting. Turn the find into a rule.
Waiting for a page is alert-driven monitoring. Hunting starts before the page.
Rules catch the known patterns at machine speed. Hunting feeds new rules. You want both.
Documentation is required. An undocumented hunt cannot become a lesson or a detection.

stem: An investigator wants to know whether a laptop's local firewall blocked a specific outbound address yesterday. The laptop is on and its firewall log was not cleared. Which source answers the question most directly?
choices: The host firewall log
A badge-reader report from the lobby
A printed org chart
The lunch menu
explanation: The host firewall log is the data source for blocks that host enforced. If it was forwarded to a SIEM, that copy may be better because it is harder for someone on the laptop to edit. A badge report shows a door. An org chart and a menu do not record packets.
choiceNotes: Read the firewall log, or the SIEM copy of it. That is the source that saw the block.
A badge reader records a door event. It does not record an outbound IP.
An org chart lists people. It is not a log.
The lunch menu is not a security log and does not record an outbound address.

stem: A vulnerability scan from last night and a packet capture from the same hour are both available. The question is whether a particular exploit payload actually crossed the wire, not whether the host is missing a patch. Which source can show the payload?
choices: The packet capture
The vulnerability scan, which records full packet contents by definition
A risk register entry
A policy PDF
explanation: A vulnerability scan reports missing patches and configuration findings. It does not store the packets of a later attack. A capture, if it covered that segment and that time, can show what was sent. A risk register and a policy are documents, not telemetry. If the capture does not exist, you cannot invent it from the scan.
choiceNotes: The capture is the payload source. The scan answers a different question: was the host exposed on paper.
Scanners do not keep a full recording of every later attack packet. That is not what a scan is.
A risk register tracks decisions. It does not store packets.
A policy states intent. It is not an observation of the wire.

stem: Dashboards show green for a server that investigators later find was compromised. The dashboard queried the server's own health agent, which the attacker had stopped. What is the lesson about that data source?
choices: A source running on the suspect host can be lied to. Prefer a copy the host cannot edit, such as shipped logs or network data
Green always means healthy
Health agents are the only trustworthy source
You should stop shipping logs off the host so the local view stays authoritative
explanation: If the attacker controls the host, they can stop an agent or edit a local log. Telemetry that already left the host, or that was observed from the network, does not depend on the attacker's cooperation. Green from a dead agent is not health. Stopping the off-box copy makes this failure permanent.
choiceNotes: Do not trust only the host to report on itself. Use the shipped logs and the network view.
Green from a stopped agent means the dashboard lost its source, not that the server is fine.
An on-host agent is useful and not sufficient once the host is the suspect.
Shipping logs off the box is how you keep a copy the attacker is less able to rewrite.

stem: Three sources disagree. The VPN log shows a login. The endpoint agent shows no process start at that minute. NetFlow shows a long session from the VPN address to a file server. Which interpretation is the most careful?
choices: Use the sources together. The endpoint gap may mean the agent was blind, while VPN and flow still show the session
Discard the VPN and the flow because the agent was quiet
The flow proves the file contents were encrypted
Disagreeing sources mean the investigation must stop
explanation: Correlating sources is the work. An agent that did not report is a clue about the agent, not an eraser for the VPN and the flow. Flow does not prove file contents or encryption. It proves a conversation of a certain size. Disagreement is why you have more than one source. You do not stop. You explain the gap.
choiceNotes: The VPN and the flow agree a session existed. Treat the quiet agent as a possible blind spot, not as proof of innocence.
Throwing away two agreeing sources because a third was silent is how you miss the incident.
Flow metadata does not include file contents and does not tell you they were encrypted.
Disagreement is a reason to look harder. It is not a reason to close the case.
